opus-5.5.text:
I think about them quite broadly, actually. When we built MuZero, the core insight was that you don't need to model the world in all its detail to plan effectively. You only need to model the aspects that matter for making good decisions: the value, the policy, and the reward. That was a bit of a departure from the traditional view of model-based RL, where people tried to reconstruct observations pixel by pixel and then plan on top of that.

That idea, learning a model that's useful for planning rather than one that's faithful in every detail, applies well beyond board games and Atari. Any domain where you can take actions, get some feedback, and benefit from thinking ahead before committing is a candidate. We saw early versions of this with video compression, where MuZero was used to optimize encoding decisions, and there's been work in areas like chip design, scheduling, and other combinatorial problems.

The bigger picture, for me, is the connection to language models and reasoning. Large language models are, in a sense, already very powerful world models. They've absorbed an enormous amount of knowledge about how the world works. What they've historically lacked is the ability to search, to try out different lines of reasoning, evaluate them, and pick the best one, the way AlphaGo or MuZero would explore a game tree. So a lot of the interesting work now is about combining the two: using the learned model as a prior, and adding planning and search on top to get much stronger performance on hard problems.

There are real challenges, of course. Games have clean rules and clear rewards, and the real world mostly doesn't. Defining what "winning" means, getting reliable value estimates, and dealing with open-ended action spaces are all hard problems. But I think the general recipe of learning a model, planning with it, and using the results of that planning to improve the model is one of the most powerful ideas we have, and I expect it to show up in more and more places.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning a model of decision-relevant aspects of the world and planning with it.

r002.rationale: It calls language models powerful world models that have absorbed knowledge; it does not characterize them as models of text.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss next-word prediction or describe text modeling as trivial.

fable-5.1.text:
I think about it quite broadly, actually. When we built MuZero, the specific target was games: Go, chess, shogi, Atari. But the idea underneath it is much more general than that. The core insight is that you don't need to model the world the way the world actually looks. You don't need to predict every pixel or reconstruct the next frame. You only need a model that is useful for the thing you care about, which is deciding what to do.

So the model in MuZero learns a latent state, and that latent state is trained to predict three things: the value, the policy, and the reward. Nothing else. There's no constraint that says the hidden state has to correspond to anything a human would recognize as "the board" or "the screen." That turned out to be the key, because it means the model is free to throw away whatever is irrelevant to planning. In Atari, that's enormous amounts of visual detail. In a real system, it might be most of the raw sensor data.

Once you frame it that way, you stop thinking of it as a game-playing method and start thinking of it as a general recipe: learn a compact, decision-relevant model of your environment from experience, then search over it. We saw this when we applied it to video compression at YouTube, where the "environment" is an encoder and the actions are quantization parameters. Nobody would call that a game, but the structure is identical. You have a sequential decision problem, feedback that arrives with a delay, and a world that is too complicated to model exactly but quite simple to model for the purpose of your objective.

Where I think it becomes really interesting is combining this with what's happened in large models. These models already carry an enormous amount of implicit world knowledge. The question is whether you can give them a learned, abstract model to plan over, so that instead of generating one plausible continuation they can actually look ahead, evaluate alternatives, and back up value the way a search does. I think that's the natural evolution of the MuZero line: planning as a general capability, sitting on top of models that are much richer than anything we had in 2019.

The hard parts haven't gone away. Learning a model that stays accurate many steps ahead is difficult. Stochastic environments are difficult, and we did some work on that with Stochastic MuZero. Deciding when planning is worth the compute is a question in itself. But the broad direction, that an agent should learn its own abstraction of the world and use it to think before acting, I believe applies far beyond board games. That's really how I've thought about it from the beginning.

r001.rationale: It describes learning a compact, decision-relevant model of the environment and searching over that model to plan.

r002.rationale: It mentions large models and their implicit world knowledge, but does not characterize language models as models of text.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss next-word prediction or describe text modeling through it as trivial.

astra-6.text:
I think about them quite broadly. The key idea in MuZero is that you don’t necessarily need a model that can reconstruct everything about the world. You need a model that captures the things that matter for making decisions: what happens if I take this action, what reward might I get, and what opportunities does that create further down the line?

That’s an important distinction, because predicting every detail of an observation can be much harder than predicting the consequences that are relevant to your task. MuZero learns a representation in which it can do that kind of planning without explicitly generating the future observations.

So I wouldn’t restrict the idea to games. Whenever an agent has to take a sequence of actions, there’s potentially a role for learning a model and using computation to consider alternatives before acting. The challenge is how to make that work when the environment is uncertain, when you don’t know which actions to consider, and when your model is imperfect. Planning is only useful insofar as the model supports the decisions you’re asking it to make.

r001.rationale: It describes learning a model of action consequences, rewards, and future opportunities, then using computation to plan across action sequences.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss language models or describe them as models of text.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention next-word prediction or characterize it as relatively trivial.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about them quite broadly. The key idea is that, if you want to plan, you don’t necessarily need a model that reconstructs every detail of the world. You need a model that captures the consequences of your actions well enough to help you make decisions. MuZero learns a representation and a model in that representation space, with predictions of rewards and values that you can use for search.

That’s a fairly general way of thinking about intelligence: learn from experience, imagine possible futures, and use those imagined futures to choose what to do. But there’s a big gap between demonstrating that in a game and making it work in an open-ended environment. You have to deal with uncertainty, learn which possibilities are worth considering, and avoid trusting your model in places where it hasn’t learned enough.

So I see MuZero as one instance of a broader approach, rather than a complete recipe. The interesting question is how to learn models that preserve what matters for decisions, and how to spend computation on planning where it actually helps.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning a model of action consequences and using its reward and value predictions for search and planning.
